title: Why We Have Rules
bigQuestion: How do rules help us stay safe and be fair to each other?

story.title: The Game That Fell Apart
story.kicker: A tag game stops working. Then the children make one rule together.
paragraphs: It is recess at a school in Chicago. Six children play tag. Maya is it. She runs and tags Omar. Omar says, "No! I was on the slide. The slide is safe!"
Maya frowns. "Nobody said the slide was safe." Now Lin says the tree is safe too. Ben says his shoe was untied, so it does not count. Everyone talks at once. Nobody is running now.
The game has stopped. Omar sits on the grass. Maya sits too. "This is not fun," says Lin. Ben nods. Then Maya has an idea. "Let's pick one rule. We all use the same one."
They talk. They agree: only the big tree is safe, and only for a count of five. Everyone says yes. Maya counts, "Ready, go!" The game starts again. This time, it works.
story.think: Why did the game start again after the children agreed on one rule?

lessons.title: Rules at Home
lessons.mainIdea: Families make rules to keep everyone safe and happy at home.
reading: Sofia comes home from school. She puts her shoes by the door. She washes her hands. Then she eats a snack. These are her family's rules.
A *rule* tells us what to do or what not to do. Families make rules. Grown-ups often make them. Kids can help too. Each family has its own rules.
Some home rules keep us safe. Do not touch the hot stove. Some rules help us get along. Take turns with the toys. Rules help a home feel calm.

words.d: words that tell us what to do or not do

look.title: Bedtime at Kenji's House
look.text: Look at Kenji's house at night. The clock says 8. Kenji brushes his teeth. He puts on his pajamas. His dad reads one book. Then the light goes off. Kenji knows these steps every night.
look.prompt: What rules does Kenji's family have at bedtime? What is one rule at your home?

check.q: What does a rule tell us?
choices: What to do or not do
check.why: A rule tells us what to do or what not to do.

check.q: Which rule keeps a child safe at home?
choices: Do not touch the hot stove
check.why: A hot stove can burn you. The rule keeps you safe.

check.q: Do all families have the same rules?
choices: Yes, every family is the same
No, each family has its own rules
check.why: The reading says each family has its own rules.

lessons.title: Rules at School
lessons.mainIdea: School rules help everyone learn, play and stay safe.
reading: It is morning in Room 12. Children raise their hands to talk. They walk in the hall. They line up for lunch. Everyone knows what to do.
Rules help a class work well. When one person talks at a time, all can hear. When we walk inside, nobody falls. Rules help us learn and play.

words.d: a group of children who learn together

look.title: Two Kinds of Circle Time
look.text: Picture circle time. First, everyone talks at once. It is loud. Nobody can hear the story. Now picture it again. Each child raises a hand. One child talks. Everyone hears.
look.prompt: Which circle time works better? Which rule helped?

check.q: Why do children raise their hands to talk?
choices: So one person talks at a time
check.why: When one person talks at a time, everyone can hear.

check.q: Why do we walk in the hall?
check.why: Walking inside keeps children from falling.

check.q: What do school rules help us do?
check.why: The reading says rules help us learn and play.

lessons.title: Rules on the Road
lessons.mainIdea: Road rules keep people safe when they walk, ride and drive.
reading: Ana and her mom stand at the corner. The light is red. Cars zoom by. They wait. The walk sign lights up. Now they cross.
Roads have rules too. Red means stop. Green means go. Walkers use the crosswalk. Riders wear helmets. These rules help keep everyone safe.
Drivers follow the rules. Walkers follow the rules. When everyone does, people get where they are going safely.

words.d: the marked place where people cross a street

look.title: At the Stoplight
look.text: Look at the street corner. A red light glows. A bus stops. A boy on a bike stops too. He wears a blue helmet. Then the light turns green. The bus goes. The boy rides on.
look.prompt: What rules do you see people following at this corner?

check.q: What does a red light mean?
check.why: Red means stop. Green means go.

check.q: Where should walkers cross the street?
check.why: Walkers use the crosswalk. Drivers look for people there.

check.q: Why do bike riders wear helmets?
check.why: Helmets are a road rule that keeps riders safe.

lessons.title: The Same Rule for All
lessons.mainIdea: A fair rule is the same for everyone.
reading: The class plays a game. The rule is: wait for your turn. Leo waits. Pia waits. Then the teacher's helper wants to skip ahead. "The rule is for me too," she says. She waits.
A rule is *fair* when it is the same for everyone. Big kids and little kids. New kids and old friends. Nobody gets to skip the rule. That is how we trust it.

words.d: the same for everyone, with nobody left out

look.title: Who Gets the Swing?
look.text: Look at the swings. Three children want one swing. One girl says, "I am the oldest. I go all day!" Another girl says, "Let's each swing for a count of twenty." Everyone gets a turn.

check.q: When is a rule fair?
choices: When it is the same for everyone
When only big kids use it
check.why: A fair rule is the same for everyone.

check.q: Why did the helper wait her turn?
choices: She did not like the game
The rule was for her too
check.why: She said the rule was for her too. Fair rules are for everyone.

check.q: In the swing picture, which idea is fair?
choices: Each child swings for a count of twenty
check.why: Each child gets the same turn. That is fair.

lessons.title: Oops! Fix It and Try Again
lessons.mainIdea: When a rule is broken, we fix it and try again.
reading: Jamal runs in the hall. He bumps into Rosa. Her books fall. Jamal stops. He says, "I am sorry." He helps pick up the books.
Everyone breaks a rule sometimes. That is how we learn. We can say sorry. We can help fix what went wrong. Then we try again.
Sometimes there is a *consequence*. That is what happens after we do something. Jamal walks back and walks again. Next time, he remembers to walk.

words.d: what happens after we do something
a word we say when we know we hurt someone

look.title: The Spilled Paint
look.text: Look at the art table. Grace grabs the paint too fast. Blue paint spills on Tom's picture. Tom looks sad. Grace gets a paper towel. She says sorry. She helps Tom start a new picture.
look.prompt: How did Grace fix what went wrong?

check.q: What can you do after you break a rule?
choices: Say sorry and help fix it
check.why: We can say sorry, help fix it and try again.

check.q: What is a consequence?
choices: What happens after we do something
check.why: A consequence is what happens after we do something.

check.q: What did Jamal do after he bumped Rosa?
choices: He helped pick up her books
check.why: Jamal said sorry and helped pick up the books.

lessons.title: Laws Are Rules for a Country
lessons.mainIdea: Laws are rules for a whole town, state or country.
reading: A family drives in the car. Everyone wears a seat belt. The baby sits in a car seat. This is not just a family rule. It is a law.
A *law* is a rule for everyone in a town, a state or a country. Leaders write laws. Police and judges help people follow them. Laws help keep people safe.
The United States has a big plan for its laws. It is called the *Constitution*. It was written in 1787. It still helps guide the country today.

words.d: a rule for everyone in a town, state or country
the main plan for the laws of the United States

look.title: Fair for Everyone
look.text: All are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 7, 1948
look.prompt: This says the law is the same for all people. How is that like a fair rule at school?

check.q: What is a law?
choices: A rule for a whole town, state or country
check.why: A law is a rule for everyone in a town, state or country.

check.q: Which one is a law?
choices: Wear a seat belt in the car
check.why: Wearing a seat belt is a law. The others are home rules.

check.q: What is the main plan for laws in the United States?
check.why: The Constitution is the main plan for United States laws.

lessons.title: Rules in Other Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Every country has rules, and some are different from ours.
reading: In Chicago, cars drive on the right side of the road. In London, cars drive on the left side. In Tokyo, Japan, they drive on the left too.
Every country has rules and laws. Some rules are different. Some are the same. Children go to school in many countries. People stop at red lights almost everywhere.
When we visit a new place, we learn its rules. That is a kind and safe thing to do.

words.d: a land with its own people, leaders and laws

look.title: Shoes Off, Please
look.text: Mei visits her friend's home in Japan. At the door there is a low step. Shoes sit in a neat row. Mei takes off her shoes. She puts on soft slippers. Many homes in Japan have this custom.
look.prompt: Mei learned a rule in a new place. What did she do?

check.q: Which side of the road do cars use in London?
check.why: In London, cars drive on the left side of the road.

check.q: Do other countries have rules?
choices: No, only the United States does
check.why: The reading says every country has rules and laws.

check.q: What is a kind thing to do in a new place?
check.why: Learning the rules of a new place is kind and safe.

review.q: What does a rule tell us?
choices: What to do or not do
review.why: A rule tells us what to do or not do.

review.q: How did the tag game start again in the story?
choices: The children agreed on one rule
review.why: The children picked one rule together. Then the game worked.
A fair rule is the same for everyone.

review.q: What does green mean at a stoplight?
review.why: Green means go. Red means stop.

choices: A rule for a whole town, state or country
review.why: A law is a rule for everyone in a town, state or country.

review.q: You spill juice on a friend's paper. What helps?
choices: Say sorry and help clean up
review.why: We say sorry, help fix it and try again.
